entries.title: Shape
entries.summary: Store Forge geometry and feature operations before SolidCraft executes them.
entries.keywords: Shape(kind: str, data: Any) -> None Shape values are normally returned by constructors such as Box(), Cylinder(), Hole() and Sketch.extrude(), then transformed or combined with the supported Shape methods/operators. Shape is only Forge's description of the model. SolidCraft owns the final BRep and feature history; users normally do not instantiate Shape(kind, data) directly. body = Box(80, 50, 12) kind Forge node type. Public constructors set this; normal model code should not invent kind values. data Data stored for that node type. Public constructors and methods build this payload.

entries.title: Occurrence.attach
entries.summary: Create a rigid or planar relationship from this occurrence to another component.
entries.keywords: Occurrence.attach(self, target, *, parent= , child= , offset=(0, 0), gap=0, angle=None, as_built=False) Placement should be expressed semantically between component references, such as left face to right face or one mounting frame to another, rather than as a calculated global XYZ position. The target must be another component occurrence. Supported standard anchors currently focus on rectangular component geometry; custom AnchorFrame/AnchorTopology references cover more specific datums. as_built=True requires all other relationship arguments to remain at their defaults. right = right.attach(left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT, gap=2) target Parent component occurrence to attach to. parent Attachment reference on target. Defaults to Anchor.RIGHT. child Attachment reference on this occurrence. Defaults to Anchor.LEFT. offset In-plane (u, v) offset on the parent attachment plane, in mm. Defaults to (0, 0). gap Separation along the parent anchor normal, in mm. Defaults to 0. angle Optional joint rotation in degrees. as_built When True, keep the occurrences at their existing poses and create an as-built rigid joint.

entries.title: Shape.at
entries.summary: Place a shape at absolute coordinates or align it to another Shape.
entries.keywords: Shape.at(self, x=0, y=0, z=0, *, anchor= , child= ) Use shape.at(x, y, z) for geometric placement. Box, Cylinder, Cone and Sphere support their documented anchors. Use shape.at(target) for the supported shape-to-shape CENTER alignment. Shape-to-shape alignment currently supports CENTER-to-CENTER only. at() is geometric placement/alignment; selecting a support face for a feature is the job of Shape.on(). pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at(10, 0, 5, anchor=Anchor.LEFT) centered = Sphere(5).at(body) x Absolute X coordinate in mm, or a target Shape for shape-to-shape alignment. y Absolute Y coordinate in mm. Leave at 0 when x is a target Shape. z Absolute Z coordinate in mm. Leave at 0 when x is a target Shape. anchor Datum on this primitive that is placed at the requested coordinate. Defaults to Anchor.CENTER. child Child datum for shape-to-shape alignment. Currently only Anchor.CENTER is supported.

entries.title: Shape.fillet
entries.summary: Round selected solid edges with one radius.
entries.keywords: Shape.fillet(self, radius, *, edges= ) Round one or more edges of a supported feature-based body. Fillet and chamfer use the same edge-selection forms. Edges.VERTICAL and cardinal Box edge selectors require a supported rectangular body. Named profile/vertex selectors require matching Polygon2D ids in a supported extrusion. body = Box(80, 50, 15) rounded = body.fillet(3, edges=Edges.VERTICAL) radius Fillet radius in mm. edges Edge selection. Use Edges.VERTICAL, a supported two-direction Box edge selector such as FRONT + LEFT, Edges.from_profile(...), Edges.from_vertices(...) or a non-empty sequence of XYZ edge pick points. Defaults to Edges.VERTICAL.

entries.keywords: Cone(*, d, top_d=0, h, axis= , anchor= ) Model a cone, tapered pin or lightly conical cylinder directly with SolidCraft's native solid.cone feature. Defaults to 0 for a full cone. h Length along the selected axis, in mm. axis Cone axis. Use Axis.X, Axis.Y or Axis.Z. Defaults to Axis.Z. anchor CENTER or one of the two axial end datums.

entries.title: Getting started
entries.summary: From a Python class to editable SolidCraft geometry.
entries.keywords: What SCPF does SCPF is a Python interface and compiler for native SolidCraft commands . It is not a replacement CAD kernel. You describe a model using ordinary Python; SolidCraft executes the generated commands and owns the final geometry and feature history. Install the library In the lib.py.solidcraft.forge repository and an active Python environment: python -m pip install -e ./scpf python -m unittest discover -s scpf/tests -v Your first model Define one class, give it numeric dimensions, and return the body from build() . No main() or show() is necessary. from scpf import Box, Edges class Plate: length = 100.0 width = 60.0 thickness = 10.0 def build(self): plate = Box(self.length, self.width, self.thickness) return plate.fillet(2, edges=Edges.VERTICAL) Plate() Compile, inspect, then execute Save the model as model.py . Compilation alone does not open SolidCraft. The JSON is a native command plan, not a mesh or STEP file. python -m scpf model.py --out output/model.json python -m json.tool output/model.json For a live GUI run, open SolidCraft, enable Preferences → Assistant → Let AI agents connect , and use: python -m scpf model.py --connect --new --new asks SolidCraft to replace the active design with a new, empty one before the model batch is sent. Leave it off when you deliberately want to add commands to the current design. Neither form saves the design. The CAD project also provides a separate native CLI qualification workflow. Where to continue Read Model objects first. Then read Positioning and orientation . That chapter explains the practical difference between at() , on() , Shape.attach() , Placement and Occurrence.attach() . After that, From one component to an assembly shows how separate physical parts are combined.

entries.title: Model objects and parameters
entries.summary: What a class, Shape, component and occurrence mean.
entries.keywords: A model is a normal Python class Numeric class attributes become editable SolidCraft parameters when SCPF compiles a plain model class. build() returns geometry. If a file contains exactly one public class with build() , that class is the root automatically; no trailing constructor call or launcher file is needed. from scpf import Box class Plate: length = 100.0 width = 60.0 thickness = 10.0 def build(self): return Box(self.length, self.width, self.thickness) Run that source file directly with python -m scpf plate.py --connect . The same rule lets a reusable component file serve as its standalone model while assemblies import the exact same class. If a file contains several public model classes, SCPF deliberately does not guess: finish the script with an explicit call such as Assembly() to choose the root. An explicit final call is also how you override root parameters for a particular run, for example Plate(width=80) . Arithmetic such as self.length / 2 is preserved symbolically for supported expressions; general Python computations are not automatically made parametric. Parameter intent is visible in the name SCPF distinguishes three kinds of numeric class attributes. This keeps a Python build setting from looking like a native editable CAD parameter. class Display: PANEL_COUNT = 5 # fixed constant _panel_pitch = 160.0 # Forge/build-time input opening_width = 844.0 # native model parameter Name Meaning SolidCraft parameter UPPER_CASE Fixed constant No _lower_case Forge/build-time input No lower_case Editable model parameter Yes If a public lower-case parameter is consumed only as a concrete Python value—for example through pv() —Forge emits a ModelParameterWarning . The same warning is emitted when a parameter remains native in some geometry but is also flattened into concrete occurrence placement. Such a parameter is only partly associative: editing it in SolidCraft would update only part of the model. Keep Placement coordinates symbolic or rename an intentionally build-time input with a leading underscore. Share one model parameter across child components Passing a parent parameter into several component inputs keeps one native SolidCraft parameter instead of creating component-specific duplicates. bottom = BottomBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius) roof = RoofBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius) bracket = Bracket( bracket_width=self.bracket_width, inside_corner_radius=self.corner_radius, ) Here the wooden fillets and bracket inside fillet all depend on the same corner_radius . Passing the parent parameter into the child input reuses that existing native dependency rather than creating a duplicate child parameter. Reusable component defaults stay fixed unless they are explicitly published with include= . Parent Parameters/Expressions passed into child inputs always stay symbolic and reuse the existing parent dependency. Bracket = component( CornerBracket, include=("inside_corner_radius",), ) # Or publish all public defaults explicitly: FullyEditableBracket = component(CornerBracket, include="*") This publication rule is recorded in change 0003 . Shape versus component occurrence Shape describes geometry or a feature expression ( Box , Hole , an extrusion). A component occurrence is one placed instance of a shared, editable model definition. Do not confuse a new occurrence with a new feature history. from scpf import Box, Placement, component class Block: def build(self): return Box(40, 20, 10) BlockComponent = component(Block) first = BlockComponent(placement=Placement(x=-25)) second = first.copy(placement=Placement(x=25)) assembly = first + second The two occurrences share the same Block definition. Placement is occurrence creation metadata: XYZ is absolute in the parent coordinate frame and optional rotation adds orientation. The component definition never receives placement as a model parameter. Groups are actual native parent components blocks = (first + second).group("Blocks") Grouping changes the browser hierarchy, not the geometry's orientation. At present one shared definition cannot be split among different groups. Important boundaries Associative attachment is supported for a limited set of rectangular component faces. General mates, arbitrary face queries and rotational constraints are not implemented as a complete assembly solver. Next: Positioning and orientation explains how to place geometry and component occurrences, and when at() , on() or attach() is the right choice.

entries.title: Positioning and orientation
entries.summary: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement.
entries.keywords: Which one do I use? These APIs all affect where something ends up, but they mean different things. Choose the one that matches the rule in the model. You want to… Use What it means Place or align geometry inside one part shape.at(...) Geometric placement. No joint or assembly relationship is created. Put a feature on a face of another shape feature.on(...) Within-part feature placement. The selected Faces value chooses the support or entry face. Place a feature with explicit parent/child anchors Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring. Prefer on() when a simple face is enough. Give one component occurrence an absolute pose Placement(...) Position and optional orientation at occurrence creation/copy time. No joint is created. Relate two separate physical component occurrences Occurrence.attach(...) An assembly relationship that SolidCraft stores as a native joint. The important distinction: Shape.attach() and Occurrence.attach() have the same verb but work at different levels. The first places a feature inside one part. The second relates two separate component occurrences. Start with the coordinate system X, Y and Z are model axes. A normal Box has its large base in XY and thickness along Z. A camera rotation changes only the view. It does not change the model coordinates. Also separate two levels: geometry inside one part has its own coordinates; a component occurrence has a pose in the assembly. Use at() to place or align geometry from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Cylinder pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at( 10, 0, 5, anchor=Anchor.LEFT, ) body = Box(80, 50, 12) centered_bore = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body) shape.at(x, y, z) places supported geometry at an absolute model coordinate. A primitive can use anchor=... to say which of its own datums belongs at that coordinate. shape.at(target) currently aligns CENTER to CENTER. It does not mean “put this on the top face”. For a feature on a face, use on() . Use on() for a feature on a face from scpf import Box, Depth, Faces, Hole plate = Box(100, 60, 10) hole = Hole(d=8, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL).on( plate, face=Faces.TOP, offset=(20, 0), ) plate = plate + hole on() is for a feature that belongs to an existing shape. Faces.TOP or Faces.BOTTOM selects the face where the feature starts or is supported. The offset is measured in that face. A sketch has the same idea in explicit form: Sketch(on=body, parent=Anchor.TOP) creates a named sketch on a selected body face. Shape.attach() is lower-level within-part placement from scpf import Anchor, Boss, X, Y boss = Boss(d=7, h=12, hole_d=2.5).attach( case, parent=Anchor.INNER_BOTTOM, offset=(X.MIN + 10, Y.MAX - 10), ) Use Shape.attach() only when a simple on() face does not express the required feature reference. It lets you choose explicit parent and child anchors. This does not create an assembly joint. The feature and target are still geometry inside one part. Use Placement for a component occurrence from scpf import Placement, X, Z, component @component class Panel: def build(self): return Box(160, 320, 14.5) first = Panel() second = first.copy( placement=Placement(x=160, z=20) ) upright = first.copy( placement=Placement( z=160, rotation=(X, 90), ) ) upside_down = first.copy( placement=Placement(rotation=(Z, 180)) ) Placement describes the complete pose of one component occurrence in its parent coordinate frame. XYZ is absolute. The optional rotation is one axis-angle orientation. Placement does not say that one component depends on another. It only says where this occurrence is. Use Occurrence.attach() for separate physical parts from scpf import Anchor left = Block() right = Block().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT, ) assembly = left + right Here right is a separate physical part. Its rule is not an absolute XYZ position; its left side belongs on the right side of left . That is an assembly relationship, so use Occurrence.attach() . SolidCraft stores this as a native joint. If the parent changes size, the relationship can still express which references belong together. The next chapter, From one component to an assembly , builds on this distinction. Shape.move() is a local geometry translation body = Box(40, 20, 10) shifted = body.move(x=10, y=0, z=25) move() translates supported geometry inside its current shape expression. It is not the normal way to position a component occurrence. Use Placement for occurrences. Copies can have different placements first = Panel( placement=Placement(z=160, rotation=(X, 90)) ) second = first.copy( placement=Placement(x=160, z=160, rotation=(X, 90)) ) screen = first + second The two occurrences reuse one component definition but have different placements. copy() without a placement override keeps the source Placement. Current limits Operation Current meaning Shape.at(...) Absolute geometry placement; shape-to-shape alignment is currently CENTER-to-CENTER. Shape.on(...) Supported within-part feature placement on TOP or BOTTOM. Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring. Placement(...) Absolute occurrence pose with one optional axis-angle rotation. Occurrence.attach(...) Assembly relationship between separate component occurrences.

No joint or assembly relationship is created. Put a feature on a face of another shape feature.on(...) Within-part feature placement. The selected Faces value chooses the support or entry face. Place a feature with explicit parent/child anchors Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring. Prefer on() when a simple face is enough. Give one component occurrence an absolute pose Placement(...) Position and optional orientation at occurrence creation/copy time. No joint is created. Relate two separate physical component occurrences Occurrence.attach(...) An assembly relationship that SolidCraft stores as a native joint. The important distinction: Shape.attach() and Occurrence.attach() have the same verb but work at different levels. The first places a feature inside one part. The second relates two separate component occurrences.

entries.title: Start with the coordinate system
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. X, Y and Z are model axes. A normal Box has its large base in XY and thickness along Z. A camera rotation changes only the view. It does not change the model coordinates. Also separate two levels: geometry inside one part has its own coordinates; a component occurrence has a pose in the assembly.

entries.title: Use at() to place or align geometry
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Cylinder pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at( 10, 0, 5, anchor=Anchor.LEFT, ) body = Box(80, 50, 12) centered_bore = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body) shape.at(x, y, z) places supported geometry at an absolute model coordinate. A primitive can use anchor=... to say which of its own datums belongs at that coordinate. shape.at(target) currently aligns CENTER to CENTER. It does not mean “put this on the top face”. For a feature on a face, use on() .

entries.title: Use on() for a feature on a face
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. from scpf import Box, Depth, Faces, Hole plate = Box(100, 60, 10) hole = Hole(d=8, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL).on( plate, face=Faces.TOP, offset=(20, 0), ) plate = plate + hole on() is for a feature that belongs to an existing shape. Faces.TOP or Faces.BOTTOM selects the face where the feature starts or is supported. The offset is measured in that face. A sketch has the same idea in explicit form: Sketch(on=body, parent=Anchor.TOP) creates a named sketch on a selected body face.

entries.title: Shape.attach() is lower-level within-part placement
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. from scpf import Anchor, Boss, X, Y boss = Boss(d=7, h=12, hole_d=2.5).attach( case, parent=Anchor.INNER_BOTTOM, offset=(X.MIN + 10, Y.MAX - 10), ) Use Shape.attach() only when a simple on() face does not express the required feature reference. It lets you choose explicit parent and child anchors. This does not create an assembly joint. The feature and target are still geometry inside one part.

entries.title: Use Placement for a component occurrence
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. from scpf import Placement, X, Z, component @component class Panel: def build(self): return Box(160, 320, 14.5) first = Panel() second = first.copy( placement=Placement(x=160, z=20) ) upright = first.copy( placement=Placement( z=160, rotation=(X, 90), ) ) upside_down = first.copy( placement=Placement(rotation=(Z, 180)) ) Placement describes the complete pose of one component occurrence in its parent coordinate frame. XYZ is absolute. The optional rotation is one axis-angle orientation. Placement does not say that one component depends on another. It only says where this occurrence is.

entries.title: Use Occurrence.attach() for separate physical parts
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. from scpf import Anchor left = Block() right = Block().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT, ) assembly = left + right Here right is a separate physical part. Its rule is not an absolute XYZ position; its left side belongs on the right side of left . That is an assembly relationship, so use Occurrence.attach() . SolidCraft stores this as a native joint. If the parent changes size, the relationship can still express which references belong together. The next chapter, From one component to an assembly , builds on this distinction.

entries.title: Shape.move() is a local geometry translation
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. body = Box(40, 20, 10) shifted = body.move(x=10, y=0, z=25) move() translates supported geometry inside its current shape expression. It is not the normal way to position a component occurrence. Use Placement for occurrences.

entries.title: Copies can have different placements
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. first = Panel( placement=Placement(z=160, rotation=(X, 90)) ) second = first.copy( placement=Placement(x=160, z=160, rotation=(X, 90)) ) screen = first + second The two occurrences reuse one component definition but have different placements. copy() without a placement override keeps the source Placement.

entries.title: Current limits
entries.summary: Positioning and orientation
entries.keywords: Where geometry and component occurrences go, and when to use at(), on(), attach() or Placement. Operation Current meaning Shape.at(...) Absolute geometry placement; shape-to-shape alignment is currently CENTER-to-CENTER. Shape.on(...) Supported within-part feature placement on TOP or BOTTOM. Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring. Placement(...) Absolute occurrence pose with one optional axis-angle rotation. Occurrence.attach(...) entries.title: From one component to an assembly
entries.summary: When to use a Shape, component, occurrence, anchor, relationship or group.
entries.keywords: Start with the mental model Forge separates geometry from physical parts and from relationships between parts . Most assembly code becomes much easier once those three levels are kept separate. You mean… Forge concept SolidCraft result Geometry inside one part Shape Native geometry/features in one definition One reusable physical part @component class Reusable component definition Where/how one occurrence stands placement=Placement(...) Occurrence placement One placed copy of that part Block() / copy() Component occurrence Several parts collected together a + b Assembly containing occurrences One part depends on another attach() Native SolidCraft assembly relationship/joint A named mounting reference Anchor , AnchorFrame , AnchorTopology Reference used by that relationship Browser/subassembly organisation group() Nested native component 1. A component means one physical part A component is not limited to one primitive. It is the definition of one physical manufactured item. Its build() may contain several primitives, sketches, holes, bosses, fillets and other features as long as they together describe that one part. from scpf import Box, Cylinder, component @component class MountingPlate: width = 80.0 depth = 50.0 thickness = 5.0 def build(self): plate = Box(self.width, self.depth, self.thickness) boss = Cylinder(d=16, h=12).at(0, 0, self.thickness) return plate + boss The plate and cylindrical boss are geometry/features inside one component . They do not need an assembly joint because they are not separate physical parts. Physical-part test: if the boss is machined, printed or moulded as part of the plate, keep it inside one component. If it is actually a separate brass insert pressed into the plate, make a second component and relate the two occurrences in an assembly. MountingPlate is the reusable definition. Calling MountingPlate() creates one occurrence; copy() creates another occurrence of the same definition without duplicating the feature history. 2. Put components in one assembly first = Block(placement=Placement(x=-30)) second = first.copy(placement=Placement(x=30)) assembly = first + second Here first + second means “these two component occurrences belong to one assembly”. It does not Boolean-union their solids. Same operator, different level: Shape + Shape describes supported geometric union; occurrence + occurrence builds an assembly of physical parts. placement=Placement(...) declares the pose when an occurrence is created or copied. It does not create a mechanical relationship; use attach() when another occurrence owns the relationship. 3. Use @assembly when the composition itself is reusable You do not need @assembly merely because a script contains several components. Use it when the composition itself is a reusable model object that you want to import or instantiate as a subassembly. from scpf import Anchor, assembly @assembly class BlockPair: def build(self): left = Block() right = Block().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT, ) return left + right pair = BlockPair() The component definitions remain the physical parts. BlockPair describes how those occurrences are composed. This is different from group() : an assembly expresses the model composition; grouping controls the native nested hierarchy/browser unit. 4. Use attach() when the relationship is the intent If the real rule is “the left side of this part belongs on the right side of that part”, encode that relationship instead of calculating a replacement XYZ coordinate yourself. from scpf import Anchor left = Block() right = Block().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT, ) assembly = left + right Forge records an associative attachment between the two occurrences and lowers that to the native SolidCraft relationship mechanism. The anchors say which references are related ; they are not just prettier names for a hard-coded XYZ point. This is the important rule: use an anchor when you need to describe a relationship or semantic mounting reference . Do not add anchors to every component pre-emptively. 5. Which kind of anchor? Situation Use Normal rectangular face/corner is enough Anchor.LEFT , Anchor.FRONT_TOP_RIGHT , etc. The reusable part owns a special mounting point and orientation Named AnchorFrame returned by the component's anchors() The reference must follow a particular native edge/corner topology AnchorTopology The reference exists only because of this larger assembly Assembly-owned with_anchor() , not an application-specific anchor added to the generic part Start with the simplest standard Anchor . Move to AnchorFrame or AnchorTopology only when a face/corner reference cannot express the actual mounting intent. 6. Let SolidCraft own the native relationship Forge describes the relationship; SolidCraft owns the resulting native geometry, occurrence hierarchy and joint data. Forge is not intended to grow a second general mating solver. That is also why a meaningful attach() is preferable to Forge inventing increasingly clever coordinate corrections. offset=(u, v) moves within the attachment plane, gap is normal distance between references, and angle is the relative turn around the attachment normal. These are relationship values, not a replacement global XYZ transform. There are two useful attachment modes. Normal attach() uses the chosen references to determine the relationship and placement. Use attach(..., as_built=True) when both occurrences are already in the intended pose and SolidCraft should record that existing pose as a fixed assembly relationship instead of repositioning them. 7. A group is organisation, not a relationship frame = (left + right).group("Frame") group("Frame") creates a real nested native component so the occurrences appear together in the SolidCraft browser hierarchy. Grouping does not mate, align or rotate the parts and does not replace attach() . Use a group when the collection itself is a useful named subassembly or browser unit. Do not create a group merely because two components touch. A practical decision sequence Will these features be manufactured as one physical item? Keep them in one component, even if the geometry is complex. Is something installed or manufactured separately? Give it its own component occurrence. Do you only need a deliberate occurrence pose? Supply placement=Placement(...) when creating or copying it. Should one separate part follow another semantically? Use attach() and the simplest suitable anchor. Is a standard face/corner insufficient? Define an AnchorFrame or topology-backed reference at the level that owns that meaning. Do several occurrences form a useful named subassembly/browser unit? Then use group() . After this page, the Components and assemblies chapter covers parameter sharing, offsets, custom frames, topology anchors and assembly-owned datums in detail.

entries.title: Geometry, sketches and Boolean operations
entries.summary: Solids, 2D profiles, extrusions and the CSG operators.
entries.keywords: Start with a solid Box , Cylinder and Sphere are centred on their geometric CENTER by default. Use anchor=... when a face, axial end or tangent datum should lie at the origin. For Cylinder the anchor is resolved after choosing Axis.X , Axis.Y or Axis.Z ; for example LEFT/RIGHT are the axial ends of an X-axis cylinder and BOTTOM/TOP are the axial ends of a Z-axis cylinder. from scpf import ( BOTTOM, FRONT, LEFT, RIGHT, Axis, Box, Cylinder, Sphere, ) plate = Box(80, 50, 8) board = Box(80, 50, 12).at( 0, 0, 0, anchor=FRONT + BOTTOM, ).fillet( 4, edges=[BOTTOM + LEFT, BOTTOM + RIGHT], ) pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.Z).at( 10, 10, 8, anchor=BOTTOM, ) side_pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at(-10, 0, 0) ball = Sphere(12) body = Sphere(20) & Box(30, 30, 30) centered_bore = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body) at(x, y, z) places CENTER at those coordinates unless another anchor=... is supplied. Passing another Shape instead uses shape-relative CENTER-to-CENTER placement. Forge derives the native Box corner, Cylinder base or Sphere center from the selected datum; callers do not add manual half-size corrections. Draw a 2D profile, then extrude it A Rectangle2D is a planar profile rather than a 3D body. 2D geometry is authored inside an explicit Sketch scope. Polygon2D can be created on the XY, XZ or YZ plane. from scpf import Sketch, Rectangle2D, Polygon2D with Sketch(plane="XY") as plate_sketch: Rectangle2D(80, 50) plate = plate_sketch.extrude(8) with Sketch(plane="XZ") as side_sketch: Polygon2D( [(0, 0), (40, 0), (40, 8), (8, 8), (8, 30), (0, 30)], plane="XZ", world=True, ) side = side_sketch.extrude(10) # Signed distance chooses the side of the sketch plane. backward = plate_sketch.extrude(-8) centered = plate_sketch.extrude(8, sym=True) A sketch plane affects where its axes go; changing the camera does not rotate its geometry. Leave the with Sketch(...) scope, then call sketch.extrude(...) to create 3D material. A positive distance follows the sketch-plane normal, a negative distance goes the other way, and sym=True divides a positive distance equally over both sides. Direct Rectangle2D(...).extrude(...) syntax is intentionally not supported. Select profiles when extruding a Sketch By default Sketch.extrude() uses every closed profile in the Sketch. Use profiles=[(x, y), ...] when only some closed regions should be extruded or cut. The points are fixed coordinates in the Sketch itself; users do not need SolidCraft profile indices or curve ids. from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Circle2D, Depth, Sketch board = Box(120, 80, 5, anchor=Anchor.BOTTOM) with Sketch(name="Selected holes", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as holes: seed = holes.add(Circle2D(d=8), offset=(-30, 0)) holes.rectangular_pattern( seed, count=4, spacing=20, direction=Axis.X, ) board = board - holes.extrude( Depth.THROUGH_ALL, profiles=[(-30, 0), (-10, 0), (30, 0)], exact_regions=True, ) SolidCraft 0.42 stores a successful point selection using the curves around the selected profile where possible. That lets the selection follow the profile when the saved design recomputes. exact_regions=True asks SolidCraft to use exactly the region containing each point. Profile points must be fixed finite numbers; Forge Parameters and expressions are not accepted in this field. Repeat and mirror profiles inside one Sketch Sketch.rectangular_pattern() makes a native SolidCraft sketch pattern from a profile that already belongs to the Sketch. Sketch.mirror() mirrors a profile, a pattern result or an earlier mirror result. Both methods return a Sketch result that can be passed to another supported Sketch operation. from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Circle2D, Depth, Sketch board = Box(200, 120, 8) with Sketch(name="Dog holes", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as holes: seed = holes.add(Circle2D(d=8), offset=(-40, 20)) row = holes.rectangular_pattern( seed, count=4, spacing=25, direction=Axis.X, ) holes.mirror(row, axis=Axis.X) board = board - holes.extrude(Depth.THROUGH_ALL) The same operations work with native Slot profiles. A pattern or mirror result can be used as the source of the next operation. from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Sketch, SlotCenterToCenter2D with Sketch(name="Clamp slots", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as slots: seed = SlotCenterToCenter2D((20, 20), (40, 20), 8) arm = slots.rectangular_pattern( seed, count=2, spacing=50, direction=Axis.X, ) opposite = slots.mirror(arm, axis=Axis.Y) slots.mirror(arm, axis=Axis.X) slots.mirror(opposite, axis=Axis.X) count , count2 , spacing and spacing2 may use suitable model Parameters, so those values remain editable in the saved SolidCraft design. Current native qualification covers attached Sketch(on=...) use. Pattern directions support Axis.X , Axis.Y or a fixed 2D vector. Mirrors currently support the Sketch X or Y origin axis. Per-instance pattern suppression is not supported. SolidCraft 0.42 stores the curves selected when a mirror is created. If a pattern later creates extra curves after its count changes, those new curves are not added to that existing mirror automatically. Add, subtract and intersect body = Box(50, 50, 20) tool = Cylinder(d=12, h=22).at(0, 0, 0) joined = body + tool # union, where supported cut = body - tool # difference, where supported shared = body & tool # intersection, where supported The supported compiler path depends on the operands. Native feature history and CSG trees are not interchangeable for every operation. For manufacturing features such as holes, prefer the native feature operations .

entries.title: Components and assemblies
entries.summary: Reusable definitions, occurrence transforms, grouping and attachments.
entries.keywords: One definition, several occurrences from scpf import Box, assembly, component @component class Beam: length = 100.0 def build(self): return Box(self.length, 20, 20) @assembly class BeamPair: spacing = 120.0 def build(self): left = Beam() right = left.copy(placement=Placement(x=self.spacing)) return (left + right).group("Beams") pair = BeamPair() @component marks one reusable physical part. Its build() returns the complete geometry/feature tree for that part; that tree may be made from many primitives and features. @assembly marks a class whose build() composes separate component occurrences. Both decorators return callable model objects, so normal model code stays readable as Beam() and BeamPair() . SolidCraft receives one reusable definition and multiple occurrences. A group is a native parent component in the browser, not a Boolean fusion of its children. Component parameter visibility Reusable component defaults are fixed by default. Publish selected child parameters explicitly with include= : @component(include=("inside_corner_radius",)) class CornerBracket: width = 24.0 inside_corner_radius = 4.0 def build(self): ... When a parent Parameter or expression is passed into a child input, that existing dependency stays symbolic. For example, CornerBracket(inside_corner_radius=self.corner_radius) reuses the parent design's corner_radius ; it does not create a separate CornerBracket_inside_corner_radius parameter. Occurrence placement copy() retains the source Placement when no override is supplied. copy(placement=Placement(...)) creates the new occurrence with the supplied absolute pose in the parent coordinate frame. The compiler uses creation-time copy translation where SolidCraft can represent it and a native fallback only where required. center = BeamComponent() array = center for x in (-240, -120, 120, 240): array = array + center.copy(placement=Placement(x=x)) Component attachment right = BeamComponent().attach( left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT ) marker = Marker().attach( frame, parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_RIGHT, child=Anchor.BACK_TOP_RIGHT, ) attach() is the public Forge relationship between reusable components. Anchor selects the attachment reference: a supported face, or one of the eight rectangular corners such as FRONT_TOP_RIGHT . Corner anchors compile to native SolidCraft edge/corner origins, so they follow dimension changes in a saved design. Associative in-plane attachment offset attach(offset=(u, v)) moves the child within the attachment plane. Numeric values and parameter expressions are both supported. Forge lowers a non-zero or symbolic in-plane offset to a native planar joint and keeps u and v as SolidCraft joint values, so they are re-evaluated when their parameters change. wood = Parameter("wood_thickness", 18) bracket = Bracket().attach( side, parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_LEFT, child=mount, offset=(0, -wood + 12), gap=-12, ) offset is independent of gap : the two offset values move in the attachment plane, while gap remains the normal distance between the two references. On a rectangular corner origin, the second planar value follows the selected vertical corner edge; its sign is defined by that corner frame rather than by world Z. Assembly-owned named anchors When a datum belongs to the meaning of an assembly rather than to a generic component, keep it on the assembly with with_anchor() . The anchor stores the target occurrence plus its attachment reference. Consumers resolve it by name with anchor() . frame = (left + right + bottom).with_anchor( "front_top_left", left, AnchorTopology( edge=(-6, 0, 181), on=(0, 0, 181), corner=(-6, 0, 362), z=(0, 0, -1), x=(1, 0, 0), ), ) parent = frame.anchor("front_top_left") bracket = CornerBracket().attach( parent.target, parent=parent.reference, child=bracket_reference, ) This keeps a generic Board or CornerBracket free of application-specific anchor names while a higher-level frame can expose semantic datums such as front_top_left . An assembly anchor may also carry its own symbolic offset=(u, v) . Consumers can combine that semantic offset with a fixed local correction and pass the result to attach(offset=...) . This is useful when an assembly datum follows a frame parameter such as wall thickness while the reusable part keeps a fixed mounting correction. AnchorFrame: point plus orientation An AnchorFrame describes one local attachment coordinate frame. origin gives the local point; z gives the attachment normal and x fixes the rotation around that normal. Use it when a single point or rectangular Anchor is not enough to describe how the occurrence must be oriented. from scpf import Anchor, AnchorFrame mount = AnchorFrame( origin=(0, 0, -12), z=(0, 1, 0), x=(0, 0, -1), ) bracket = CornerBracket().attach( side_board, parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_LEFT, child=mount, ) There are two ownership patterns. If the datum is an intrinsic part of a reusable component, expose it with anchors() and refer to it by name. If the frame exists only because of a particular assembly or mounting choice, construct the AnchorFrame in that assembly and pass it directly to attach() . This keeps application knowledge out of the generic component definition. @component class Sensor: def anchors(self): return { "connector": AnchorFrame( origin=(12, 0, 4), z=(1, 0, 0), x=(0, 0, 1), ) } def build(self): return Box(24, 12, 8) sensor = Sensor().attach(panel, child="connector") For an unrotated occurrence, Forge lowers an AnchorFrame directly into the native joint.create reference as point , z and x ; it does not create a persistent visible joint.origin . Named frames on explicitly rotated occurrences currently use the native origin fallback so SolidCraft owns the transform. A direct AnchorFrame on an explicitly rotated occurrence is not supported yet. AnchorTopology: follow an edge or corner AnchorTopology is a named component datum that stays attached to native SolidCraft topology. edge picks an edge, on selects its adjacent planar face and corner optionally chooses one endpoint. The coordinates are selection picks; SolidCraft keeps the selected edge, face and endpoint by topology name as the design changes. from scpf import AnchorTopology, Box, component @component class Board: def anchors(self): return { "mount": AnchorTopology( edge=(-20, 50, 5), on=(-20, 50, 10), corner=(-20, 0, 5), z=(0, 1, 0), x=(0, 0, 1), ) } def build(self): return Box(40, 100, 20) This is useful for references such as the straight tangent edge beside a fillet: if dimensions move that edge, the joint can follow it without freezing the original XYZ point. The current implementation supports named or direct AnchorTopology values on non-rotated occurrences. A direct topology anchor is useful when the datum belongs only to one assembly rather than to the reusable component. SCPF deliberately does not transform topology picks itself. SolidCraft joints remain an internal implementation detail; Forge does not expose a separate public Joint object. What to test in an assembly Check the native command list for one component.create per shared definition, expected occurrence.copy counts, and native translate , axis and angle parameters for rotated occurrences. Separately verify native SolidCraft geometry and its bounding dimensions before trusting an assembly image.

entries.keywords: Unit tests for Python behavior The library's tests under scpf/tests/ cover model objects, feature compilation, reusable components and rotation validation. Tests should check component names, requested positions, the orientation axis and angle, and feature ordering. A regression can preserve a known good JSON fixture when command ordering is part of the contract. Native geometric verification The CAD model repository runs a separate SolidCraft CLI workflow for native geometry, editable history, STEP output, measurements and screenshots. Read the saved SolidCraft occurrence transforms , not just whether a command ran successfully. A valid Python object or syntactically valid command plan is not evidence that the final solid occupies the correct plane or has no collision. Keep implementation and docs in sync When placement syntax changes, add tests for the exact generated native commands before documenting it as supported. Named principal-axis rotation is supported; chained rotations are still not.
